title: Trump Directs Federal Contractors to Flag Congressional Oversight Requests to the White House
snippet: President Donald Trump signed an executive order requiring government contractors to report congressional document requests and block privileged records, setting up a legal battle with incoming Democratic committee chairs.
content:
WASHINGTON — President Donald Trump has signed an executive order requiring all federal contractors and subcontractors to immediately notify the White House of any information requests coming from Congress, instructing them to withhold any materials the administration deems protected by executive privilege.

Under the new directive, companies that fail to comply face severe penalties, including the cancellation of existing government contracts or suspension from bidding on future federal work. Trump framed the mandate as a defense mechanism against lawmakers, asserting in the order that Capitol Hill investigators are "harassing private companies" to obtain confidential executive branch information.

Escalating Battle Over Congressional Oversight

The move comes as Democrats prepare to take control of both chambers of Congress following the recent midterm elections. Capitol Hill leaders are readying aggressive oversight inquiries into the administration's policy execution, its handling of the Jeffrey Epstein investigation files, and the personal business dealings of the Trump family.

Rep. Robert Garcia, D-Calif., who is positioned to head the House Oversight Committee next term, recently dispatched document preservation letters to key administration figures and family members, including Vice President JD Vance, Donald Trump Jr., Eric Trump, Jared Kushner, and White House Chief of Staff Stephen Miller.

"Oversight Democrats have been investigating the potential corruption, self-dealing, and abuses of power that have funneled billions of dollars to the Trump family as Americans struggle with rising costs," Garcia wrote in letters sent to Trump's sons, while also targeting Miller regarding accountability for executive branch immigration enforcement efforts.

Legal Hurdles and Executive Privilege Pushback

The executive order expands on a separate directive issued earlier by White House Counsel Will Scharf, who ordered federal agencies to pre-screen executive employee testimony meant for Capitol Hill. Scharf also suggested that certain Democratic oversight tactics could cross into criminal conduct—a claim that drew swift criticism from opponents who accused the White House of attempting to shield itself from constitutional accountability.

Legal experts expect the executive order to face swift courtroom challenges, particularly if the administration attempts to force private contractors to defy formal congressional subpoenas. While executive privilege allows presidents to protect specific confidential communications, federal courts have traditionally stepped in to adjudicate disputes between the executive branch and congressional oversight powers.
